_updated: 1998-07-06
- Prefers recovery-spin routes with fewer junctions because they make it easier to maintain a genuinely easy effort; recovery spins will start from the park side of town going forward (coach/athlete, 1998-07-06).
- Easy/recovery days should be protected even when the schedule becomes busy, using relaxed breathing as the key effort cue (coach/athlete, 1998-07-06).

_updated: 1998-07-06
- On rolling rides, hold a steady endurance effort on climbs rather than surging; keep breathing conversational and cadence comfortable through the middle hours (coach/athlete, 1998-07-06).
- For rides over two hours: drink one bottle per hour, eat a small amount every 30 minutes, and have a slightly larger breakfast when sustained climbing is planned; rehearse this on easy rides first (coach/athlete, 1998-07-06).
- In exposed headwinds, tuck lower on the bars and move the snack schedule earlier to stabilize energy in the final hour; monitor hand and shoulder comfort during longer low-position stints as weekly volume rises (coach/athlete, 1998-07-06).

_updated: 1998-07-06
- On the second day of back-to-back rides, mild leg heaviness has cleared after about 20 minutes of easy spinning; this is currently considered a normal build response and requires no adjustment (athlete/coach, 1998-07-06).
- If second-day leg heaviness persists beyond the first 30 minutes, shorten that ride rather than push through accumulated fatigue (coach/athlete, 1998-07-06).
- A final riser recently felt harder than usual, attributed to a headwind after a long day on the feet rather than declining fitness (athlete/coach, 1998-07-06).
- Breathing remained relaxed throughout a recovery spin on the lower-junction route, consistent with the intended easy effort (athlete, 1998-07-06).
